fields.h1: John Newton: From Slave Trader to “Amazing Grace”
fields.meta_title: John Newton: From Slave Trader to Amazing Grace
fields.description: The man who wrote “Amazing Grace” had been a slave trader, saved by a mercy he never got over. The story behind the world’s best-loved hymn.
fields.body_html:
“Amazing grace, how sweet the sound, that saved a wretch like me.” It is the best-known hymn in the English language, sung by millions who have never heard the story behind it. But those words were not written by a comfortable poet imagining sin from a distance. They were written by John Newton, a man who had been a slave trader — who had bought and sold human beings, who had sunk to the depths of blasphemy and cruelty, and who was rescued by a grace so undeserved that he could never stop marvelling at it. Newton’s life is one of the most powerful testimonies in history to the truth that no one is beyond the reach of God’s mercy. “The saying is trustworthy... that Christ Jesus came into the world to save sinners, of whom I am the foremost” (1 Timothy 1:15) — Newton believed it because he had proved it.

A wretch indeed

Newton was born in London in 1725. His godly mother, who taught him the Scriptures, died when he was six, and the boy drifted far from anything she had hoped for him. Pressed into the navy, flogged for desertion, and later handed over into the brutal service of a slave dealer in Africa, he sank into misery and degradation, at one point himself little better than a slave. He became, by his own later confession, a man who mocked God, corrupted others, and grew hardened in wickedness. He was, in the fullest sense, a wretch.

By his own account he had thrown off all restraint and religion, delighting to blaspheme and to lead others astray. Few would have picked him as a future minister of the gospel. But God had not finished with him. As Paul wrote of himself, God would make Newton an example of his “perfect patience... as an example to those who were to believe in him for eternal life” (1 Timothy 1:16).

The storm that turned him

The great turning point came in 1748, aboard a ship caught in a violent storm on the Atlantic. As the vessel filled with water and seemed sure to sink, the hardened Newton, to his own surprise, cried out to God for mercy. The ship survived, and Newton dated his awakening to that night. It was not yet a full conversion — his change was gradual, and he continued for a time in the slave trade even after his awakening, to his lasting grief — but God had laid hold of him, and the long work of grace had begun.

Over the following years Newton’s faith deepened, his conscience awoke to the horror of the trade he had been part of, and he eventually left the sea altogether. The Psalmist’s testimony became his own: “He drew me up from the pit of destruction, out of the miry bog, and set my feet upon a rock... And he put a new song in my mouth, a song of praise to our God” (Psalm 40:2–3). The new song, for Newton, would one day become the world’s most famous hymn.

From the slave ship to the pulpit

The transformation was so complete that the former slave trader became a clergyman. After years of study, Newton was ordained and became a pastor, eventually serving in the town of Olney and later in London. There he preached the gospel of the grace that had saved him, cared tenderly for his people, and poured his experience into hymns written for his congregation — among them “Amazing Grace,” a hymn that is really his autobiography set to music.

Newton never got over the wonder of his own salvation, and it made him a preacher of extraordinary tenderness toward sinners. He knew from the inside that grace reaches the worst, and so he held out hope to everyone. His whole life proclaimed Paul’s words: “But by the grace of God I am what I am” (1 Corinthians 15:10). He had become a new creation: “the old has passed away; behold, the new has come” (2 Corinthians 5:17).

The epitaph he wrote for himself

Newton understood his own story so clearly that he composed his own epitaph, and it is one of the great summaries of the gospel ever written. He directed that his gravestone read: “John Newton, Clerk, once an infidel and libertine, a servant of slaves in Africa, was, by the rich mercy of our Lord and Saviour Jesus Christ, preserved, restored, pardoned, and appointed to preach the faith he had long laboured to destroy.”

Every word is weighed. He does not hide his past — infidel, libertine, servant of slaves — but neither does he end there, for the whole point is the “rich mercy” that met him. It is the very pattern Paul describes: “we ourselves were once foolish, disobedient, led astray... But when the goodness and loving kindness of God our Savior appeared, he saved us, not because of works done by us in righteousness, but according to his own mercy” (Titus 3:3–5). Newton’s tombstone preaches the gospel to this day.

A voice against slavery

In his later years Newton did something few former slavers ever did: he spoke out publicly against the trade he had once plied. He wrote a searching account of its evils and lent his testimony to the movement to abolish the slave trade, becoming a mentor to those who fought for its end. His repentance was not merely private sorrow but public action, using his own shameful history as a weapon against the very evil he had served.

This is grace bearing fruit. The man who had trafficked in human beings became a witness against that trade, his transformed conscience turned to the good of others. It is a striking picture of what conversion means — not only a changed standing before God but a changed life, working now for justice and mercy where once it worked for cruelty and gain. Grace does not merely forgive the past; it turns the forgiven into instruments of good.

The pastor and letter-writer

Newton’s converted heart made him one of the most tender and wise pastors of his age, and his influence spread far beyond his own pulpit. At Olney he formed a close friendship with the gifted but deeply melancholy poet William Cowper, and together they produced a collection of hymns for their congregation — songs of experience meant to help ordinary believers sing their faith. Out of that collaboration came “Amazing Grace” and many other hymns still sung today, and Newton’s steady faith was a lifeline to his troubled friend through seasons of despair.

Newton also became famous for his letters. He carried on a vast correspondence, counselling believers near and far with a wisdom and gentleness born of his own long experience of grace. His letters are full of good sense, humility, and comfort, and many were later gathered and published, becoming classics of pastoral counsel that guided readers who never met him. He had a rare gift for pointing struggling Christians away from themselves and toward the mercy of God — the very mercy that had rescued him — and for treating the weakest believer with patience, remembering how far he himself had been carried.

Why his story still matters

John Newton died in 1807, having lived to see the British slave trade abolished. He never lost his wonder at grace, reportedly saying near the end that though his memory was almost gone, he remembered two things: that he was a great sinner, and that Christ was a great Saviour. That is the whole of his testimony, and the whole of the gospel.

There is a particular power in the fact that the hymn the world loves best came from such a source. When we sing “that saved a wretch like me,” we are singing Newton’s literal autobiography — the confession of a man who had trafficked in human lives and been reached by a grace he could never deserve or repay. The hymn endures not merely because its tune is beautiful but because its truth is universal: every one of us is a wretch saved by grace, if we are saved at all, and Newton simply felt it more keenly than most because he had fallen further than most.

Newton’s life stands as a permanent answer to anyone who believes they have sinned too greatly to be forgiven. If grace could reach a hardened, blaspheming slave trader and make him a minister of the gospel and a hymn-writer whose song still leads the world in praise, then no one is beyond its reach. “Where sin increased, grace abounded all the more” (Romans 5:20). Newton proved it, and his amazing grace is the same grace offered to every sinner still — sweet enough to save a wretch like him, and like us. However far you have wandered, however dark your past, the grace that reached John Newton on a sinking ship can reach you where you are; you have only to look to the Saviour, as a poor slave trader once did, and be amazed.
